title: Failure
hookLine: Peter failed and was trusted again
tomorrow: Thomas wouldn't believe without touching. was that so wrong?

lines: A FIRE OF COALS, AND A DENIAL.
cards: A missed penalty gets replayed forever. Peter's worst night does too.

He swore he'd die before he'd deny Jesus, and hours later he's warming his hands at a fire of coals in the high priest's courtyard, telling a servant girl he doesn't know the man. Then comes the strange part.
At the very end of John's Gospel, after the resurrection, there's another fire of coals, on a beach, with Jesus cooking breakfast. Why would John light the same fire twice?

teach.h: HOT COALS, A FISH, AND BREAD.
teach.b: Peter and the others have fished all night and caught nothing. A man on the shore tells them where to cast, the net fills, and Peter jumps into the sea.
On land, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "they saw hot coals lying, and a fish laid thereon, and bread." After they eat, Jesus asks Peter a question.
Simon, son of John, lovest thou me? Then he asks again. Then a third time, and Peter is grieved: "Lord, thou knowest all things: thou knowest that I love thee."
Here's the puzzle solved, the way many readers hear it. Three denials by one fire; three questions by another. Jesus doesn't pretend the courtyard never happened.

teach.h: THE SAME SMOKE, A NEW YES.
teach.b: He brings Peter back to the smell of the same kind of smoke and lets him say yes as many times as he said no.
Then he gives him a job: "Feed my sheep." The man who failed loudest isn't benched. He's handed the flock.
Here's one for a friend tonight: John records no scolding for the denial. Just a fire, breakfast, and three questions.
Catholics carry that pattern into confession: name the failure plainly, hear it forgiven, and walk out with work still to do. Failure in this story isn't where the trust ends.

how: Catholics bring their failures to the sacrament of confession, naming them to a priest, hearing the words of absolution and receiving a small penance; John 21 is read at Mass in the Easter season.

o: proof you were never good enough
a mistake that can never be undone
falling short of what you meant to do

games.q: two fires in John — tap the pairs.
p: where Peter said he didn't know him
a fish and bread on hot coals

s: after the denials, Peter was quietly replaced
Jesus asks him three questions, then hands him the flock: feed my sheep.
Peter had sworn he would never deny Jesus
he said he'd die first, and that same night he denied knowing him.
in John, Jesus scolds Peter on the beach for the denial
no scolding is recorded: a fire, breakfast, and three questions.

games.q: your teammate missed the deciding penalty last season. now it's a shootout again, and she asks to take one. by John 21's pattern, what does the coach do?
o: talk it through with her, then hand her the ball.
bench her until she proves herself in practice.
hand her the ball and never mention the miss.
games.why: Jesus doesn't skip the failure (three questions by a fire) and doesn't bench Peter: feed my sheep. trusted again.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one failure you still replay, just a few words. Under it, write two more: trusted again.
If you pray, you can hold the paper and say Peter's line, Lord, thou knowest that I love thee; if not, let the second line sit under the first for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Failure. Falling short of what you swore you'd do. In Peter's story, it's the place the trust starts over.

orig.note: Greek, John 18:18 and 21:9: a charcoal fire, the word John uses for both fires.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: trusted again, because Peter got the flock after the fire, not before. Until tomorrow.
